title: Adding Information to Noun Phrases: Apposition and Reduced Clauses
summary: Expand noun phrases with defining and supplementary apposition, and/or constructions, namely and that is, reduced participle relatives, and to-infinitive postmodifiers. Match punctuation, voice and time reference to the intended meaning, especially in academic and professional writing.
learningObjectives: Distinguish defining apposition from supplementary noun phrases and punctuate each accordingly.
Add precise explanation with and, or, namely and that is without obscuring what the added phrase identifies.
Choose -ing, past participle or being + past participle reduced clauses by active, passive and ongoing meaning.
Use infinitive modifiers and non-defining participle phrases when they genuinely preserve reference and time relationships.

explanation.heading: Apposition: identifying or extra information
explanation.body: Apposition places two noun phrases next to each other when both identify the same person or thing. Supplementary apposition adds an aside and is normally marked by commas or pauses: Amira Khan, the project coordinator, presented the results. Defining apposition identifies which person is meant and ordinarily has no comma: my colleague Amira. Punctuation therefore reflects the same distinction found in defining versus non-defining relative clauses.
explanation.example: The architect Elise Morgan will introduce our guest, a specialist in public transport.

explanation.heading: And, or, namely and that is
explanation.body: A coordinated expression with and may present two roles held by one person: our manager and mentor. Or can supply an alternative name or description: the aurora, or northern lights. Namely introduces an exact instance or enumeration; that is restates or explains a description in different terms. Both often take commas in supplementary position, but neither is merely a decorative substitute for any relative clause.
explanation.example: The pilot will cover two risks, namely unreliable power and delayed deliveries.

explanation.heading: Reduced defining relative clauses
explanation.body: An -ing clause typically reduces an active defining relative (people working remotely), while a past-participle clause typically reduces a passive one (samples collected last week). These modifiers generally follow the noun they describe. Not every relative can be shortened: a form change must preserve who does what, time relationships and intended meaning; words like who, which and a form of be are not universally removable.
explanation.example: The data collected overnight are awaiting review, and the team analysing them will report tomorrow.

explanation.heading: Being + past participle marks ongoing passive action
explanation.body: A postmodifying being + past participle phrase can make a passive process in progress explicit: the bridge being inspected this week. In contrast, the bridge inspected last week may describe a completed inspection or identify which bridge is meant. Context can create overlap, but do not erase being when the ongoing interpretation is essential.
explanation.example: The instruments being calibrated today cannot yet be released for use.

explanation.heading: Infinitive and supplementary participle modifiers
explanation.body: Infinitives can qualify a noun, often identifying a prospective action, duty or opportunity: the next person to speak, a plan to modernise the library. The infinitive does not always mean purpose; decide its relation to the noun. In written narrative, supplementary -ing or -ed clauses are often set off by commas or dashes: The director, speaking from Brussels, confirmed the dates. Such clauses add information rather than restrict which director is meant.
explanation.example: The proposal, revised after consultation, gives residents more time to respond.

left.label: Defining: identify the name
left.example: My teammate Sofia will lead the workshop.
left.note: Sofia specifies which teammate is being discussed; no comma is needed.

right.label: Supplementary: extra role
right.example: Sofia, our newest teammate, will lead the workshop.
right.note: The name identifies the person; the appositive adds the role.

comparisons.title: Active, passive and ongoing passive reduction

left.label: Active -ing
left.example: The volunteers sorting donations wear blue badges.
left.note: The volunteers actively sort the donations.

right.label: Passive -ed
right.example: The donations sorted yesterday have been counted.
right.note: The donations receive the action; the shorter form identifies them.

examples.sentence: The scientist Mara Lewis will introduce the device.
examples.note: Mara Lewis identifies which scientist is meant; this is defining apposition.

examples.sentence: Mara Lewis, a specialist in robotics, will introduce the device.
examples.note: The appositive adds background information about an already named person.

examples.sentence: The audit covers two locations, namely the depot and the clinic.
examples.note: Namely lists the two specific locations announced by the prior noun phrase.

examples.sentence: The machines being repaired today will be inspected again tomorrow.
examples.note: Being repaired describes an ongoing passive process.

examples.sentence: The next candidate to be interviewed is waiting outside.
examples.note: A to-infinitive passive clause qualifies the next candidate.

commonMistakes.incorrect: My teammate Nia, is presenting today.
commonMistakes.correct: My teammate Nia is presenting today.
commonMistakes.why: Do not separate the complete subject, including the defining name Nia, from its verb with a comma.

commonMistakes.incorrect: The documents filing yesterday were misplaced.
commonMistakes.correct: The documents filed yesterday were misplaced.
commonMistakes.why: Documents receive the filing action, so a passive past participle is needed.

commonMistakes.incorrect: The two options, for example Monday and Tuesday, are the only available dates.
commonMistakes.correct: The two options, namely Monday and Tuesday, are the only available dates.
commonMistakes.why: Namely introduces the exact two options; for example would imply a non-exhaustive illustration.

commonMistakes.incorrect: The instrument calibrating at the moment cannot be used.
commonMistakes.correct: The instrument being calibrated at the moment cannot be used.
commonMistakes.why: The instrument receives an ongoing calibration; use being + past participle.

studyTips: Underline the two noun phrases in an apposition and decide whether the second identifies the referent or adds supplementary information before adding commas.
Expand each reduced relative clause back into a full who/which clause and verify active versus passive voice and time reference.
Test namely against that is: does the second expression name all intended items, or explain an equivalent term?

exercises.prompt: Choose the correctly punctuated sentence; the person is already identified by their full name.
choices: Dr Lena Brooks, the department head, will attend.
Dr Lena Brooks the department head, will attend.
Dr Lena Brooks, the department head will attend.
exercises.feedback: A supplementary noun phrase is enclosed by commas when the sentence continues.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence gives the exact two items, rather than merely examples?
choices: The kit contains two tools, for example pliers and a wrench.
The kit contains two tools, namely pliers and a wrench.
The kit contains two tools, such as pliers and a wrench.
exercises.feedback: Namely introduces a complete specification of the two tools.

exercises.prompt: Select the reduced relative clause in which the noun receives the action.
choices: The staff checking the files are busy.
The manager supervising the team is away.
The files checked yesterday are in the archive.
exercises.feedback: Checked is a past-participle modifier with passive meaning: the files were checked.

exercises.prompt: An inspection is in progress now. Which phrase makes ongoing passive meaning explicit?
exercises.feedback: Being inspected signals an ongoing action performed on the turbine.

exercises.prompt: Complete the noun phrase: "Rita Gomez, ___, will chair the meeting." Use the three-word appositive our new coordinator.
exercises.feedback: Our new coordinator is a supplementary noun phrase identifying the same person.

exercises.prompt: Complete the reduced active clause: "The people ___ (wait) outside have appointments." Write one -ing word.
exercises.feedback: Waiting corresponds to people who are waiting.

exercises.prompt: Complete the reduced passive clause: "The samples ___ (freeze) overnight are ready for analysis." Write the past participle.
exercises.feedback: Frozen is a passive participle describing the samples.

exercises.prompt: Fill the two-word passive progression phrase: "The roof ___ (repair) this week is unsafe to enter." Use being plus a past participle.
exercises.feedback: Being repaired clearly signals work currently in progress on the roof.

exercises.prompt: Correct the clause without changing passive meaning: The invoices processing yesterday were paid today.
acceptedAnswers: The invoices processed yesterday were paid today.
exercises.feedback: Invoices receive the processing; a passive past participle is required.

exercises.prompt: Correct punctuation only. Anya is already uniquely identified: Anya, our lead designer will present the prototype.
acceptedAnswers: Anya, our lead designer, will present the prototype.
exercises.feedback: A non-defining appositive must be followed by its closing comma.

exercises.prompt: Correct the exhaustive list: The three departments, such as finance, operations and research, will report on Friday.
acceptedAnswers: The three departments, namely finance, operations and research, will report on Friday.
exercises.feedback: Namely matches the exact identification of all three departments; such as suggests examples.

exercises.prompt: Correct the ongoing passive relative: The parcels shipping right now will arrive tomorrow.
acceptedAnswers: The parcels being shipped right now will arrive tomorrow.
exercises.feedback: Parcels are being shipped by someone; use being shipped rather than the active shipping.

speakingExercises.prompt: Introduce a named colleague without extra commas. Facts: My colleague / Nia / leads the workshop.
acceptedAnswers: My colleague Nia leads the workshop.
speakingExercises.feedback: Nia is defining apposition identifying the colleague.

speakingExercises.prompt: Add supplementary apposition. Facts: Nia / our training manager / leads the workshop. Include the appositive between commas.
acceptedAnswers: Nia, our training manager, leads the workshop.
speakingExercises.feedback: Our training manager adds information about Nia.

speakingExercises.prompt: Name exactly two subjects. Facts: The seminar covers two topics / namely / privacy and accessibility.
acceptedAnswers: The seminar covers two topics, namely privacy and accessibility.

speakingExercises.prompt: Say the active reduced relative. Facts: The engineer / monitoring the pumps / is on duty.
acceptedAnswers: The engineer monitoring the pumps is on duty.
speakingExercises.feedback: Monitoring is active: the engineer does the monitoring.

speakingExercises.prompt: Say the passive reduced relative. Facts: The equipment / delivered this morning / is upstairs.
acceptedAnswers: The equipment delivered this morning is upstairs.

speakingExercises.prompt: Say the ongoing passive reduced relative. Facts: The bridge / being inspected today / is closed.
acceptedAnswers: The bridge being inspected today is closed.
speakingExercises.feedback: Being inspected describes an ongoing passive action.

speakingExercises.prompt: Use an infinitive modifier. Facts: The next speaker / to address the panel / is Mei.
acceptedAnswers: The next speaker to address the panel is Mei.
speakingExercises.feedback: To address qualifies the next speaker.

speakingExercises.prompt: Correct aloud: "The results analysing yesterday were promising." Use a past participle with passive meaning.
acceptedAnswers: The results analysed yesterday were promising.
speakingExercises.feedback: Results are analysed, so use the passive participle analysed.

listeningExercises.audioText: The final report, revised after the consultation, will be published on Monday.
listeningExercises.prompt: What happened to the report before publication?
listeningExercises.feedback: Revised is a passive participle providing additional information about the report.

listeningExercises.audioText: Our guest Dr Farah Malik will explain the findings during the afternoon session.
listeningExercises.feedback: The name following our guest specifies which guest is meant.

listeningExercises.audioText: The devices being tested this afternoon will not be shipped until tomorrow.
listeningExercises.prompt: Transcribe the four-word phrase that describes an ongoing passive process.
listeningExercises.feedback: Being tested this afternoon expresses current passive testing.

listeningExercises.audioText: The exhibition includes three local crafts, namely weaving, pottery and woodcarving.
listeningExercises.prompt: How many crafts does the speaker name?
listeningExercises.feedback: The list following namely specifies exactly three crafts.

listeningExercises.audioText: The new director, a former research scientist, will visit the centre next week.
listeningExercises.prompt: What earlier role did the director have?
listeningExercises.feedback: A former research scientist is supplementary apposition.

listeningExercises.audioText: The students arriving early may enter the laboratory before the others.
listeningExercises.feedback: Arriving early is an active participial modifier restricting the group.

listeningExercises.audioText: The equipment stored in the basement has already been inspected.
listeningExercises.prompt: Transcribe the four-word phrase specifying where the equipment was kept.
listeningExercises.feedback: Stored in the basement is the complete reduced passive modifier.

listeningExercises.audioText: There are two improvements to make, namely clearer instructions and shorter forms.
listeningExercises.prompt: Transcribe the two-word phrase naming the second improvement.
listeningExercises.feedback: Shorter forms is the second of the two specifically named improvements.
